content.overview: Section 209 provides that where, upon information in his possession or otherwise, the Registrar or inspector has reason to believe that books and papers of a company or relating to the key managerial personnel or any director or auditor or company secretary in practice are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he may, after obtaining an order from the Special Court or Magistrate for that purpose, enter and search the place where such books are kept and seize them. Seized books are retained only for the period the section allows and then returned, subject to taking copies or extracts.
content.glance: Reason to believe books may be destroyed/falsified/secreted → order from Special Court or Magistrate → enter, search and seize; return within statutory period; preservation power, not adjudication on merits.
content.study: Where, upon information in his possession or otherwise, the Registrar or inspector has reason to believe that the books and papers of a company, or relating to the key managerial personnel or any director or auditor or company secretary in practice if the company, are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted, he may, after obtaining an order from the Special Court for the seizure of such books and papers, enter and search the place or places where such books or papers are kept and seize such books and papers. Current-law framing: establish reason to believe regarding destruction, falsification or secretion; obtain order from Special Court (or Magistrate as the section provides); enter, search and seize; retain only for the permitted period and return, taking copies as allowed. Seizure preserves evidence; it does not decide the merits of any allegation.

sections.heading: Trigger
sections.body: Reason to believe that books and papers of the company or relating to KMP, director, auditor or CS in practice are likely to be destroyed, mutilated, altered, falsified or secreted.

sections.heading: Order
sections.body: Prior order from the Special Court (or Magistrate as provided) for seizure.

sections.heading: Search and Seize
sections.body: Enter and search the place where books are kept and seize them.

sections.heading: Return
sections.body: Seized records retained only for the period the section states, then returned, subject to copies or extracts.

examples.title: Imminent destruction
examples.body: The Registrar has credible information that the company’s statutory registers are about to be destroyed. After obtaining an order from the Special Court, he may enter the place, search and seize the books under s. 209.

examples.title: Seizure is not a finding of guilt
examples.body: Books are seized under s. 209. That preserves them for inspection or investigation; it is not a determination that any offence has been committed.

hypotheticals.question: May the Registrar seize books under s. 209 without any court order?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 209 requires an order from the Special Court (or Magistrate as the section provides) before entry, search and seizure.

distinctions.title: Search and seizure (s. 209) vs conduct of inspection (s. 207)
distinctions.left: Court-ordered seizure where books may be destroyed or falsified
distinctions.right: Duty to produce and assist during ordinary inspection; entry on reasonable grounds without seizure order

misconceptions.trap: Any inspection automatically allows the Registrar to seize and keep the company’s books indefinitely.
misconceptions.correction: Seizure under s. 209 requires reason to believe books may be destroyed or falsified and a prior court order. Retention is only for the period the section allows, after which books are returned.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 209 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Test reason to believe. II. Confirm court order. III. Apply search and seize. IV. Check return period. V. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Belief facts; order status; seizure scope; return; precise relief.

enhancement.definition: Section 209 allows the Registrar or inspector, on reason to believe that books may be destroyed or falsified, to obtain a court order and then enter, search and seize those books, returning them within the statutory period.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Evidence preservation by court-authorised seizure protects the integrity of inspection and investigation without converting seizure into adjudication.
essentialIngredients: Reason to believe books may be destroyed, falsified or secreted
Order from Special Court or Magistrate
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 209 is the preservation-by-seizure power in the inspection chapter.
examples: Seizure is not a finding of guilt
enhancement.problemApplication: Test belief; confirm order; apply seizure and return.
